summary: Explains why the Connection-less Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (CLDAP) specification, RFC 1798, was never advanced beyond Proposed Standard, and recommends that it be moved to Historic status.

plainLanguage.summary: CLDAP was designed for small directory lookups without setting up a connection, but it did not become widely deployed. This memo explains why RFC 1798 should move to Historic status.

questions: why was connectionless ldap made historic
why was cldap moved to historic
subtitle: Why the connection-less LDAP specification was moved to Historic status.

tldr.problem: CLDAP had not become widely deployed, lacked several security and functional features, and had no active effort to update its obsolete references.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3352 explains the issues and recommends moving RFC 1798 to Historic status.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3352 obsoletes RFC 1798 and points readers interested in connection-less directory access toward experiments with LDAP over UDP and other alternatives.

today: RFC 3352 is Informational and obsoletes RFC 1798, recommending that it be moved to Historic status. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 3352.

sections.title: What CLDAP Was Designed to Do
sections.content:
Connection-less Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (CLDAP), defined in RFC 1798, was published in 1995 as a Proposed Standard. It targeted applications needing small amounts of directory information.

It avoided setting up and closing a connection and the bind and unbind operations used by connection-oriented directory protocols. It was designed to complement LDAP version 2.
sections.plainLanguage: CLDAP offered small directory lookups without first establishing a connection. It was intended to complement LDAP version 2.

sections.title: Reasons It Did Not Advance
sections.content:
Seven years after publication, CLDAP had not become widely deployed on the Internet. The memo lists limited functionality (anonymous and read-only access with small results), no integrity or confidentiality protection, inadequate internationalization, limited extensibility, and a lack of multiple independently developed implementations.

Its normative references included obsolete technical specifications. Without updating the specification, the Historic reference to LDAPv2 meant CLDAP could not remain on the standards track.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo lists limited capabilities, missing security protections, and a lack of independent implementations as likely issues. Its references also pointed to specifications that were no longer current.

sections.title: Recommendation and Further Work
sections.content:
The LDAP Extensions Working Group was chartered in 1997 to update CLDAP, but it was concluding without producing an update. No standardization effort remained.

The memo says the community remained interested in connection-less directory access but considered further experimentation necessary, especially to address security. It recommends that RFC 1798 be moved to Historic and suggests experimenting with LDAP over UDP/IP and other alternatives.
sections.plainLanguage: Because no update was being produced, the memo recommends retiring RFC 1798 to Historic. It says further experimentation is needed for connection-less directory access, including its security.

references.text: Young, A., "Connection-less Lightweight Directory Access Protocol", RFC 1798, June 1995.
Yeong, W., Howes, T., and S. Kille, "Lightweight Directory Access Protocol", RFC 1777, March 1995.
